```{r, include = FALSE}
# the full examples run when the package is built; CRAN checks skip them for time
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = identical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN"), "true"), collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(bayescompR)
```

bayescompR runs entirely in the R interpreter. Its cost model differs from
compiled Stan: every operation on a tape node has a fixed overhead of a few
microseconds, while the arithmetic inside a vectorized node runs at the
speed of R's compiled internals. Fast models therefore do a few large
operations rather than many small ones. This vignette shows how to measure
the cost of a model and how to write models that run fast.

## Measuring

The cost of inference is the number of gradient evaluations times the cost
of one gradient. NUTS reports the leapfrog steps per iteration in
`n_leapfrog__`.

```{r}
time_grad <- function(model, reps = 200) {
  u <- rep(0.1, bayescomp_dim(model))
  t <- system.time(for (i in seq_len(reps)) bayescomp_grad_log_prob(model, u))[["elapsed"]]
  1e6 * t / reps   # microseconds per gradient
}
```

## Vectorize

The same regression written with a loop and vectorized:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
N <- 500
x <- rnorm(N)
y <- 1 + 2 * x + rnorm(N)
d <- list(N = N, x = x, y = y)
loop <- bayescomp_model("
data { int N; vector[N] x; vector[N] y; }
parameters { real a; real b; real<lower=0> s; }
model { for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(a + b * x[n], s); }", data = d)
vec <- bayescomp_model("
data { int N; vector[N] x; vector[N] y; }
parameters { real a; real b; real<lower=0> s; }
model { y ~ normal(a + b * x, s); }", data = d)
glm <- bayescomp_model("
data { int N; vector[N] x; vector[N] y; }
parameters { real a; real b; real<lower=0> s; }
model { y ~ normal_id_glm(to_matrix(x), a, [b]', s); }", data = d)
c(loop = time_grad(loop, 10), vectorized = time_grad(vec), glm = time_grad(glm))
```

The loop creates thousands of tape nodes per gradient; the vectorized
statement creates a handful. In compiled Stan the difference is small; in
bayescompR it is two orders of magnitude.

Guidelines:

* Use vectorized sampling statements and functions (`y ~ normal(mu, s)`
  with vector `mu`), not loops over observations.
* Use the GLM densities (`normal_id_glm`, `bernoulli_logit_glm`,
  `poisson_log_glm`, `neg_binomial_2_log_glm`, `categorical_logit_glm`,
  `ordered_logistic_glm`) for regressions.
* Index with integer arrays (`theta[group]`) instead of looping over
  groups.
* Compute data only quantities in `transformed data`; they are evaluated
  once.
* Prefer `*_cholesky` parameterizations (`multi_normal_cholesky`,
  `lkj_corr_cholesky`) to avoid decompositions at every evaluation.
* Loops over parameters are fine when their count is small; the overhead
  is per operation, not per element.

## Gradient free kernels

Metropolis and slice sampling evaluate the log density without the tape,
which is cheaper than a gradient. They need many more evaluations, but on
small models with expensive gradients they can be competitive.

## Parallel chains

Chains run one after another by default. Pass `cores` to run them in
parallel, or set the `mc.cores` option once per session, which every
function that takes `cores` uses as its default. Chains run in forked
processes; on Windows, where forking is not available, they run in a socket
cluster whose workers load the installed package and print their progress
when they finish. Each
chain has its own random number stream derived from `seed`, so the draws are
identical whether the chains run in parallel or not.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 4, cores = 4, seed = 1)
# or, for the whole session
options(mc.cores = 4)
fit <- bayescomp_sample(model, chains = 4, seed = 1)
```

The other samplers that take `cores` (for example `bayescomp_gibbs()`,
`bayescomp_pdmp()` and `bayescomp_riemannian()`) follow the same default, and
`bayescomp_smc()` and `bayescomp_ep()` use it for the particle moves and the
site updates.

## Native backends

For models whose likelihood is written as loops the interpreter overhead
dominates, and the native backends help most. Measured on an Apple silicon
laptop for a normal linear regression with N = 5000, one gradient takes
939 ms in R and 2.7 ms with Cranelift when the likelihood is a loop over
observations, and 0.56 ms in R and 0.23 ms with Cranelift when it is
vectorized. NUTS on the vectorized model runs about 1.7 times faster end to
end, since the sampler itself stays in R. Vectorize first; then try a
native backend:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(bayescompRCranelift)
m <- bayescomp_model(code, data, backend = "cranelift", allow_fallback = TRUE)
bayescomp_validate_backend(m)
```

## How the AD tape is kept fast

For developers, the implementation choices that matter most:

* Tape lists in the `.ad` environment are detached before element
  assignment and reattached afterward, so R modifies them in place instead
  of copying the whole tape at each node (which made gradients quadratic in
  the number of nodes).
* Densities are fused nodes with analytic partial derivatives, one node per
  sampling statement.
* The constraining transforms of lower and upper bounds are single nodes.
* Value only evaluations disable the tape entirely.
